newsitem.title: UK: Dollar/yen mired near lows amid broad yen gains.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/yen mired near lows amid broad yen gains.

text.p: The dollar was mired near the six-month low it set against the yen amid concern Japan's trade surplus will be a focus at the the Group of Seven leading industrial nations later this month.
A barrage of comments from Japanese officials indicating they viewed the dollar's two-yen slump in Asia as excessive lifted the U.S. currency off its lows.
Broad-based yen strength, which has seen the Japanese currency also surge to a nine-month high against the mark, will, however, prevent the dollar clawing back too much ground, analysts said.

"The bottom line is that the yen is strong across the board and the overall bias is very much to buy yen on any dips" said Mark Geddes, the treasury economist at ABN Amro. "US comments which suggested that Japan's trade surplus will be a point of discussion for the G-7 triggered it."

The dollar was quoted at 112.35/40 yen at 0755 GMT, after falling as low as 111.80 yen in Asia, its weakest since November 25. 1996. That compared with 115.65/75 late Friday in Europe. The U.S. currency was at 1.7219/29 marks, from 1.7308/18 Friday.
The yen strengthened to 65.20 per mark, its best showing since August 1996. It was last at 65.22/25 from 66.72/75.

Concern about the potential for renewed trade frictions between the U.S. and Japan were triggered after U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said Friday the Clinton administration was concerned about the potential for an upturn in Japan's trade surplus with the U.S. and a downturn in some of America's major export sectors.

The comments triggered speculation that Japan's trade surplus will be a focus for discussion by the Group of Seven leading industrial nations when they meet in Denver between June 20-22. Japan's trade surplus with the U.S. leapt 163 percent in April from a year earlier to 831.48 billion yen.
Expectations such concern will mount before the release of the Japanese trade report on June 17 and the G-7 summit triggered sales of dollars, driving the U.S. currency down more than two yen.

Japanese officials were quick to step in to curb yen gains. Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said Japan will do its utmost to achieve currency stability, which would contribute to a sustainable economic recovery.
Tsutomu Makino, Japan's Vice Minister of International Trade and Industry also weighed in saying Monday's rise in dollar/yen was excessive.

Also, Japanese Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa said he hoped for stable currency trading and said he was not aware that Japan's trade surplus would become a specific topic of discussion at the G-7 meeting in Denver.
While these comments supported the dollar for the time being, traders said pressure on the U.S. currency will likely reemerge before next week.

"The comments out of Japan may hold the dollar for a bit, there is a danger the dollar will crack the 111.80 level and move on down to 111.50 before the trade figures or the G7," said Juergen Lindemann, a senior trader at IBJ.

The dollar was steadier in Europe, though off the 39-month high it set against the mark Friday. Traders expect the dollar to remain supported against the mark given persistent concern that European economic and monetary union will either be launched by a broad group of countries or delayed.

Traders are looking to French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn to reveal the new government's views on the European Union's budget stability pact later Monday. -Swaha Pattanaik, London Forex Desk +44 171 542 6284
